h: From Repeated Exiles to Lasting Redemption

p: וַיִּגַּשׁ אֵלָיו יְהוּדָה.
— Judah approached him.
בְּמִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה אִיתָא עַל זֶה: הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים נְאֻם הַשֵּׁם,
— Midrash Rabbah applies to this: “Behold, days are coming, declares Hashem,
וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ — זֶה יְהוּדָה, בַּקּוֹצֵר — זֶה יוֹסֵף וְכוּלֵי.
— when the plowman”—Judah—“will draw near the reaper”—Joseph, and so forth.
לִכְאוֹרָה אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לְהַפָּרָשָׁה רַק מַה דִּכְתִיב וְנִגַּשׁ, שֶׁהֲרֵי הַפָּסוּק מְדַבֵּר בַּגְּאוּלָּה הָעֲתִידָה.
— Seemingly its sole connection to our portion is the word “draw near,” since the verse concerns the future redemption.
אָמְנָם הַפָּרָשָׁה שָׁם מַתְחֶלֶת הֲלוֹא כִבְנֵי כוּשִׁיִּים וְגוֹמֵר,
— However, that passage begins, “Are you not like the children of Cush,” and so forth.
וְשָׁמַעְתִּי מֵהָרַב הַקָּדוֹשׁ זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מְרַמֵּז עַל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית שֶׁנִּקְרָא כּוּשִׁי,
— I heard from the holy Rabbi, of righteous and holy memory, that this alludes to a blemish of the covenant, termed “Cushite.”
וְהוּא הֵיפֶךְ בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהוּא מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם,
— This is the opposite of Joseph’s aspect: he is a vehicle for the attribute of “the righteous one, foundation of the world,”
וְנִקְרָא יְפֵה תוֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה, שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ גּוּף נָקִי וּמְהוּדָּר.
— and is called “handsome in form and handsome in appearance,” having a pure and beautiful body.
וְכֵן כָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ, (רו ב): יְפֵה נוֹף — דָּא אִיהוּ יוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק, דִּכְתִיב וַיְהִי יוֹסֵף יְפֵה תוֹאַר וְגוֹמֵר.
— The holy Zohar on this portion, 206b, likewise states: “beautiful in elevation”—this is Joseph the righteous, for it is written, “Joseph was handsome in form,” and so forth.
וְכֵן כָּתוּב לְהַלָּן, (רז סוֹף עַמּוּד א): נָפִיק מִינֵּיהּ עַנְפָא חֲדָא שַׁפִּירָא בְּחֵיזוּ וְכוּלֵי, וּמַאן אִיהוּ? דָּא יוֹסֵף וְכוּלֵי.
— Further, at the end of 207a: a branch beautiful in appearance emerges from him, and so forth. Who is it? Joseph, and so forth.

p: וְאָמַר הַכָּתוּב: כִּי הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה וַהֲנִעוֹתִי וְגוֹמֵר, וְלֹא יִפּוֹל צְרוֹר אָרֶץ.
— Scripture says, “For behold, I command, and I shall shake,” and so forth, “yet no pebble shall fall to the ground.”
שֶׁזֶּה תַּכְלִית הַגָּלֻיּוֹת, שֶׁיִּתְבָּרְרוּ כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל, אִישׁ מֵהֶם לֹא נֶעְדָּר,
— The purpose of the exiles is that every Jewish soul should be refined, not a single one missing,
שֶׁכּוּלָּם בִּכְלַל מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וְעַמֵּךְ כּוּלָּם צַדִּיקִים. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְלֹא יִפּוֹל צְרוֹר אָרֶץ.
— all included in “your people are all righteous.” This is the meaning of “no pebble shall fall to the ground.”
וְאַחַר זֶה נֶאֱמַר הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ — זֶה יְהוּדָה וְכוּלֵי,
— It then says, “Behold, days are coming, and the plowman shall draw near”—Judah, and so forth,
בְּמוֹשֵׁךְ הַזָּרַע — זֶה יוֹסֵף, שֶׁמָּשַׁךְ זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו וְהוֹרִידוֹ לְמִצְרַיִם וְכוּלֵי.
— “with the sower”—Joseph, who drew his father’s offspring down to Egypt, and so forth.
שֶׁגָּלוּת הָרִאשׁוֹן הָיָה לְמִצְרַיִם, שֶׁהִיא עֶרְוַת הָאָרֶץ, וּלְשָׁם נִמְשְׁכוּ עַל יְדֵי יוֹסֵף שֶׁבָּא רִאשׁוֹנָה לְמִצְרַיִם.
— The first exile was to Egypt, the nakedness of the land, and they were drawn there through Joseph, who first came to Egypt.
וְאִיתָא (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ד): יוֹסֵף יָרַד לְמִצְרַיִם וְגָדַר עַצְמוֹ מִן הָעֶרְוָה, וְנִגְדְּרוּ כָּל הַזְּכָרִים בִּזְכוּתוֹ.
— Shir HaShirim Rabbah, chapter 4, teaches that Joseph descended to Egypt and guarded himself against sexual immorality, and all the males were guarded through his merit.
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁמָּשַׁךְ זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אָבִיו וְכוּלֵי, הַיְינוּ שֶׁיְּתוּקְּנוּ כּוּלָּם שֶׁיִּהְיוּ בִּכְלַל וְעַמֵּךְ כּוּלָּם וְגוֹמֵר.
— “He drew his father’s offspring,” and so forth, means that they would all be repaired and included in “your people are all,” and so forth.
וּבֶאֱמֶת נִתְבָּרְרוּ שָׁם הַכֹּל.
— Indeed, all were refined there.

p: אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּצְרְכוּ עוֹד לַגָּלֻיּוֹת, עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם,
— Nevertheless, further exiles were necessary, in the sense of “a righteous person falls seven times and rises.”
וְהוּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ שֶׁבַע נְפִילוֹת, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִתְבָּרְרוּ הֵיטֵב בְּמִדָּה זוֹ.
— There are seven falls through which they are thoroughly refined in this attribute.
וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אָקִים אֶת סוּכַּת דָּוִד הַנּוֹפֶלֶת,
— Thus it says, “On that day I will raise the fallen booth of David.”
וְעַל שֵׁם זֶה נִקְרָא מָשִׁיחַ בַּר נַפְלֵי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין צו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב).
— For this reason Messiah is called Bar Nafli, “son of the fallen,” as stated at the end of Sanhedrin 96b.
וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה עה): שֶׁרָאָה יִצְחָק בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ וְכוּלֵי, אָמַר לוֹ בֹּא וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ בְּרָכָה שֶׁל גָּלֻיּוֹת וְכוּלֵי.

— Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 75, likewise relates that Isaac foresaw through divine inspiration, and so forth, and said: “Come, and I shall bless you with a blessing concerning the exiles,” and so forth.
וּמַה הֵן הַבְּרָכוֹת? בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ, וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע וְכוּלֵי.
— What are these blessings? “From six troubles He will deliver you, and in seven no evil will touch you,” and so forth.
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה דְּאִיתָא (מִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה נָשֹׂא פָּרָשָׁה י): לְכָךְ כְּתִיב שֵׁשׁ פְּעָמִים לְמִי, כְּנֶגֶד שִׁשָּׁה גָּלֻיּוֹת וְכוּלֵי.
— Similarly, Midrash Rabbah on Naso, chapter 10, teaches: “To whom” is written six times, corresponding to six exiles, and so forth.
וְאֵלּוּ הֵן: מִצְרַיִם תְּחִלָּה, וְאַחַר אַשּׁוּר, בָּבֶל, מָדַי, יָוָן וֶאֱדוֹם וְכוּלֵי.
— These are: first Egypt, then Assyria, Babylonia, Media, Greece, and Edom, and so forth.
וְזֶהוּ בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אַחַר הַהַצָּלָה הָיָה עוֹד צָרָה, שֶׁהוּצְרְכוּ לְבֵירוּר אַחַר בֵּירוּר.
— Thus, “From six troubles He will deliver you”; even after deliverance, further trouble arose, because refinement after refinement was required.
אַךְ בְּשֶׁבַע, שֶׁזֶּה מְרַמֵּז לְמִלְחֶמֶת גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג, שֶׁכְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה שְׁבִיעִית,
— But “in seven” alludes to the war of Gog and Magog, corresponding to the seventh attribute.
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר לֹא יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע, שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ לֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד שׁוּם רַע בָּעוֹלָם, שֶׁזֶּה יִהְיֶה תְּשׁוּעַת עוֹלָמִים.
— Of this it says, “No evil will touch you,” for thereafter no evil will remain in the world: this will be everlasting salvation.
וְנֶאֱמַר זֶה לְיַעֲקֹב, שֶׁאֶצְלוֹ גַּם כֵּן מָצִינוּ שֶׁבַע צָרוֹת,
— This was said to Jacob, in whose life we likewise find seven troubles,
שֶׁנֶּחְשְׁבוּ (בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא סוֹף פָּרָשַׁת מִקֵּץ וְהוּבָא בְּרַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי): צָרַת לָבָן, צָרַת עֵשָׂו, צָרַת רָחֵל, צָרַת דִּינָה, צָרַת יוֹסֵף, צָרַת שִׁמְעוֹן.
— enumerated in Midrash Tanchuma at the end of Miketz and cited by Rashi: the troubles of Laban, Esau, Rachel, Dinah, Joseph, and Simeon.
וְהֵם כְּנֶגֶד מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּשֵׁשׁ צָרוֹת יַצִּילֶךָּ, שֶׁגַּם אַחַר שֶׁהָיָה הַצָּלָה הָיָה עוֹד צָרָה.
— These correspond to “From six troubles He will deliver you,” since even after deliverance another trouble arose.
וּבְשֶׁבַע לֹא יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע — נֶגֶד צָרַת בִּנְיָמִין, שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹשַׁע תְּשׁוּעַת עוֹלָמִים,
— “And in seven no evil will touch you” corresponds to Benjamin’s trouble, after which he attained lasting salvation,
שֶׁבָּא לְמִצְרַיִם וְרָאָה אֶת יוֹסֵף בִּגְדוּלָּה,
— coming to Egypt and seeing Joseph in his greatness,
וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם — חַיִּים שֶׁלֹּא בְּצַעַר וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּיֵצֶר הָרָע, (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב סֵדֶר אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ה).
— “Jacob lived in the land of Egypt”—a life without suffering and without the evil inclination, as stated in Seder Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 5.
וּמַעֲשֵׂה אָבוֹת סִימָן לַבָּנִים, שֶׁכֵּן בְּמִלְחֶמֶת גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג לֹא יִגַּע בְּךָ רָע, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַיְשׁוּעָה לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד.
— The patriarchs’ deeds foreshadow their descendants’ experience: likewise in the war of Gog and Magog, “no evil will touch you,” for salvation will last forever.
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר אַחַר כָּךְ וְשַׁבְתִּי אֶת שְׁבוּת עַמִּי וְגוֹמֵר, וְלֹא יִנָּתְשׁוּ עוֹד מֵעַל אַדְמָתָם וְגוֹמֵר.
— Thus it later says, “I will restore My people’s captivity,” and so forth, “and they will never again be uprooted from their land,” and so forth.
וְכֵן בַּמִּדְרָשׁ הֵבִיא הַרְבֵּה דִּמְיוֹנוֹת מִפְּסוּקֵי פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ לְעִנְיַן הֶעָתִיד,
— The Midrash similarly draws many parallels between this portion’s verses and the future,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה צג): וַיִּתֵּן אֶת קוֹלוֹ בִּבְכִי — כְּשֵׁם וְכוּלֵי, כָּךְ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֵינוֹ גוֹאֵל אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ בְּכִיָּה וְכוּלֵי.
— as at the end of Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 93: “He raised his voice in weeping”—just as, and so forth, likewise the Holy One, blessed be He, redeems Israel only through weeping, and so forth.
וְכֵן יוֹסֵף קְטַנָּן שֶׁל שְׁבָטִים וְכוּלֵי, לִכְשֶׁיָּבֹא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְיוֹכִיחַ כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד לְפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא וְכוּלֵי,
— Likewise: Joseph, the youngest of the tribes, and so forth—when the Holy One, blessed be He, comes and rebukes each person according to who he is, and so forth.
וְהַיְינוּ לֶעָתִיד.
— This refers to the future.
וְכֵן בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ, (רח ב): בְּזִמְנָא דְּקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא יוֹקִים לָהּ לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵי,
— Likewise, the holy Zohar on this portion, 208b: when the Holy One, blessed be He, raises the Community of Israel, and so forth,
כְּתִיב וּמֵעַמִּים אֵין אִישׁ אִתִּי, וּכְתִיב הָכָא וְלֹא עָמַד אִישׁ אִתּוֹ וְגוֹמֵר, וְכַדּוֹמֶה.
— it says, “Of the peoples, no man was with Me,” while here it says, “No man stood with him,” and so forth, and similar parallels.
וְכֵן (בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ) חָשַׁב: כָּל שֶׁאֵירַע לְיוֹסֵף אֵירַע לְצִיּוֹן וְכוּלֵי.
— Midrash Tanchuma at the end of this portion likewise enumerates: everything that happened to Joseph happened to Zion, and so forth.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Miketz 10: ““And El Shaddai”: Why did Yaakov see fit to bless them with El Shaddai? To teach that many sufferings had passed over Yaakov. Even in his mother’s womb Esav struggled with him, as it says, “The children struggled within her.” … He fled from Esav to Lavan and spent twenty years there amid many troubles, as it says, “By day scorching heat consumed me.” After he left, Lavan pursued him to kill him. When he escaped him, Esav came and again sought to kill him, and he lost that entire gift on his account. When he escaped Esav, the trouble of Dinah came upon him; after Dinah’s trouble, Rachel’s trouble. After all these troubles he sought to rest a little, and Yosef’s trouble came upon him. Scripture cries: “I was not tranquil, nor quiet, nor at rest.” Afterward came Shimon’s trouble, and then Binyamin’s trouble. Therefore he prayed by El Shaddai: “May He who said ‘Enough’ to heaven and earth say ‘Enough’ to my sufferings.””

paragraphs.text: Seder Eliyahu Rabbah 5: “Why did Yaakov merit a life without suffering and without the evil inclination in this world, of what the Holy One will give the righteous in the future? Because he sat in the house of study from his youth until his old age, and was proficient in Scripture and Mishnah, halakhot and aggadot, as it says, “Yaakov was a wholesome man, dwelling in tents.” … Immediately the compassion of the Holy One was stirred, and He gave Yaakov seventeen good years near the end of his life, resembling the World to Come. p: וְהוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, דְּהַגְּאוּלָּה תִּהְיֶה עַל יְדֵי שְׁנֵי הַמְּשִׁיחִים,
— As we explained, redemption will come through the two messiahs:
מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף שֶׁיְּבָרֵר כָּל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהֵם בִּכְלַל וְעַמֵּךְ כּוּלָּם וְגוֹמֵר.
— Messiah son of Joseph will refine all Jewish souls, who are included in “your people are all,” and so forth.
אַךְ בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף הוּא שֶׁלֹּא פָּגַם כְּלָל, וְיֵשׁ פְּרָטֵי נְפָשׁוֹת שֶׁפָּגְמוּ.
— Yet Joseph’s aspect is never to have incurred any blemish, whereas some individual souls have incurred blemishes.
וְעַל זֶה בָּא בֶּן דָּוִד, שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה,
— For this comes the son of David, who established the yoke of repentance.
וּמָשִׁיחַ הוּא יָחִיד שֶׁעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ מוֹחֲלִין לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ, (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב יוֹמָא פו:),
— Messiah is the individual who repents and for whose sake the entire world is forgiven, as stated in Yoma 86b,
וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּכְנִיס הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּהַכְּלָל.
— meaning that he will instill a thought of repentance within the community.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי לֹא יִמְחֲלוּ לְכָל הָעוֹלָם בִּכְדִי.
— As we explained, the whole world would certainly not be forgiven without cause.
וְזֶה נִזְכָּר בִּיהוּדָה, הַקִּלְקוּל בְּעֵר וְאוֹנָן וְהַתִּיקּוּן עַל יְדֵי פֶּרֶץ, שֶׁהוּא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ הַמָּשִׁיחַ.
— This is recorded concerning Judah: the corruption of Er and Onan, and its repair through Perez, who is the light of King Messiah.
וְזֶה עִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנִּדְרַשׁ פָּרָשִׁיּוֹת אֵלּוּ עַל הַגְּאוּלָּה.
— This explains why these portions are expounded as referring to redemption.
וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (רז ב): דָּוִד מַלְכָּא אִיהוּ חַי, וְקוּרְבָא דִילֵיהּ לְחֵי הָעוֹלָמִים וְכוּלֵי.
— The holy Zohar 207b states: King David is alive, and his closeness is to the Life of the worlds, and so forth.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּחֵי הָעוֹלָמִים נִקְרָא בְּחִינַת יוֹסֵף, כַּנּוֹדָע.
— “Life of the worlds” denotes Joseph’s aspect, as is known.
וְדָוִד נִכְתַּב עָלָיו מִקּוֹדֶם הַפְּגָם, וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִתְבָּרֵר דָּוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל חַי וְקַיָּם,
— David’s blemish was first recorded, but afterward it was clarified that “David, king of Israel, lives and endures,”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה ח): בְּאוֹתוֹ שָׁעָה חָיָה דָּוִד.
— as stated at the beginning of Shemot Rabbah, chapter 8: at that moment David came to life.
וְזֶה מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב וְנִגַּשׁ חוֹרֵשׁ — זֶה יְהוּדָה, בַּקּוֹצֵר — זֶה יוֹסֵף,
— This is “the plowman”—Judah—“will draw near the reaper”—Joseph,
וּכְעֵין מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וְקָרַב אוֹתָם אֶחָד אֶל אֶחָד לְךָ לְעֵץ אֶחָד.
— paralleling “Bring them near to each other, to become one stick for you.”
שֶׁנִּדְרַשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה צח): הַתְקִינוּ עַצְמְכֶם לַגְּאוּלָּה. מַה כְּתִיב אַחֲרָיו? וְעָשִׂיתִי אֶתְכֶם לְגוֹי אֶחָד וְגוֹמֵר.
— Bereishit Rabbah, chapter 98, expounds: prepare yourselves for redemption. What follows? “I shall make you one nation,” and so forth.
וְאָז יִתְבָּרְרוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמִדַּת צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם, דְּכָל מַאן דְּאִתְגְּזַר וְכוּלֵי, (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב כג א).
— Then all Israel will be refined in the attribute of “the righteous one, foundation of the world,” for everyone who is circumcised, and so forth, as stated in Zohar, Part II 23a.
וְשַׁבָּת מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁבּוֹ גַּם כֵּן הַזְּמַן לְתַקֵּן פְּגָם זֶה,
— Shabbat is a foretaste of the World to Come, and it too is a time for repairing this blemish.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (שָׁם צב א): דְּשַׁבָּת רָזָא דִבְרִית,
— As the holy Zohar states there, 92a: Shabbat is the mystery of the covenant,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ הִתְגַּלּוּת מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא,
— containing a revelation resembling the World to Come,
דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים.
— for all Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says, “Your people are all righteous.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Yehudah Aryeh Leib Alter, Sefat Emet, Vayigash 8:3: “Through acceptance of His kingship everything can be repaired. This is the essence of Judah’s aspect, named for acknowledging the truth: through acknowledgment the world has repair and counsel. The aspects of Judah and Joseph are two. There is a righteous man who is a man of rest, upon whom the Creator bestows a spirit of holiness without toil of soul and flesh. And there is a righteous man who stands in his righteousness while many paths and crooked places pass over him, until he arrives at the right place. Both must exist, and they are the aspects of the working days and of holy Shabbat: Joseph is the aspect of Shabbat, and Judah the days of labor. Therefore the Midrash alludes, ‘The plowman shall draw near the reaper’: plowing is Judah’s labor, and Joseph is the reaper, ready to reap after completion. At the end of Judah’s deeds it says, ‘He approached him’: having completed the labor, he came to cleave to Joseph the righteous, who is Shabbat. Then he saw and understood that both are true, and ‘the jealousy of Ephraim departed.’”

Shmuel Bornsztain, Shem MiShmuel, Vayishlach 4:8–9: “Something of this exists in every Jew, for both of these are in Shabbat, ‘Remember’ and ‘Keep,’ the Shabbat of the night and the Shabbat of the day. The Shabbat of the night is ‘Keep,’ which is in the heart. It is the time when love and cleaving to their Father in Heaven awaken in all Israel, as they cast off the yoke of the many reckonings and the burden of the thirty-nine labors, and all are crowned with new souls. This is the repair of the heart’s blemish of love for externals. The Shabbat of the day is ‘Remember,’ which is in the mind. On Shabbat there is a great illumination from the two messiahs, and were Israel to keep it they would be redeemed at once. At any rate, each person, according to how he keeps Shabbat in ‘Remember’ and ‘Keep,’ repairs in some measure the blemish of mind and heart within him. With this we can explain the verse, ‘In plowing and in harvest you shall rest.’ According to the Midrash at the beginning of Vayigash, ‘The plowman shall draw near the reaper,’ the plowman is Judah and the reaper is Joseph. The verse therefore alludes that by keeping Shabbat one merits a taste of the two messiahs, who are called the plowman and the reaper.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar II, 92a: ““Remember the Shabbat day to sanctify it”: this is the mystery of the holy covenant. Because all the sources of the body’s limbs are established in this covenant, it includes everything. Similarly, Shabbat comprises the Torah, and all the Torah’s mysteries depend upon it. Observing Shabbat is like observing the entire Torah: whoever keeps Shabbat is as though he kept the whole Torah.”
